subject: biology

items.q: Which statement gives the meaning of the term habitat as it is used in ecology?
items.correct: The place in which a community, species, population or single organism lives.
items.misconception: The role that a species plays in its ecosystem, including what it feeds on.
items.why: In everyday speech 'habitat' is used loosely for an animal's whole way of life, and wildlife programmes describe 'habits and habitat' together, so students merge the place with the role. The distinction between habitat (place) and niche (role) is not drawn until later in the course. A habitat is a place, described by geographical location, physical location and the type of ecosystem. The role a species plays is a different idea (its niche); two species can share a habitat while doing very different things in it.
items.specStatementText: Habitat is the place, not the role or the residents
items.random_wrong: A large region of the Earth that shares one type of climate, such as tundra.

items.q: Marram grass (Ammophila arenaria) grows on the seaward slopes of sand dunes along the Atlantic coasts of western Europe. Which of the following is a description of the habitat of marram grass?
items.correct: The seaward slopes of foredunes in the coastal sand dune ecosystems of western Europe.
items.misconception: All of the marram grass plants that grow on one particular dune system on the coast of Wales.
items.why: Population, community and habitat are introduced together as a block of definitions, and students recall 'a group of ... living in an area' for all three without separating the living group from the place it occupies. A population is the group of organisms of one species; the habitat is the place, which can be described by its geographical location, physical location and ecosystem type.
items.specStatementText: Habitat is the place, not the role or the residents
items.random_wrong: The marram grass, sea holly, sand lizards and dune beetles living together on a dune.

items.q: In dry, windy weather the leaves of marram grass roll inwards, so that the stomata, which lie in grooves on the inner surface, open into an enclosed space lined with hairs. How does this help marram grass to survive on a sand dune, where water drains away quickly?
items.correct: Humid air is trapped around the stomata, lowering the water vapour concentration gradient and slowing transpiration.
items.misconception: Sea spray and dew collect inside the rolled leaf and are absorbed through the stomata, supplying the plant with water.
items.why: Students see water lying on leaves after rain and have watered houseplants by spraying them, and they know leaves lose water through stomata, so they assume the pores can also take water in. Water is absorbed by the roots. Leaf and stem adaptations of plants in dry habitats (rolled leaves, hairs, thick cuticle, spines) reduce water loss by transpiration; drip tips in the rainforest shed water from the leaf surface rather than collecting it.
items.specStatementText: Adapted to the non-living conditions: dunes and mangroves
items.random_wrong: The hairs increase the surface area from which water evaporates, so that the leaf is cooled more effectively in the sun.

items.q: The grey mangrove (Avicennia marina) grows in tidal mud that is waterlogged and almost free of oxygen. From its horizontal roots it sends up pneumatophores, which project vertically out of the mud into the air. What is the function of the pneumatophores?
items.correct: They let oxygen diffuse from the air into the root tissues buried in anaerobic mud.
items.misconception: They anchor the tree against the tidal currents by spreading its weight across the soft mud.
items.why: Students most often see photographs of the arching stilt roots of Rhizophora, which do give support, and they apply the same function to every kind of aerial root because anchorage is the only root function they associate with a swampy site. Different mangroves have different aerial roots with different functions. Rhizophora's stilt roots support the tree in soft mud; Avicennia's thin pneumatophores are aerial roots for gas exchange, supplying oxygen for respiration to roots in mud that contains almost none.
items.specStatementText: Adapted to the non-living conditions: dunes and mangroves
items.random_wrong: They absorb water vapour from the humid air above the mud to supplement the uptake by the roots.

items.q: Mangrove trees grow with their roots in seawater, which has a much lower water potential than the soil water available to most land plants. Which statement describes an adaptation of mangroves to the high salinity of their habitat?
items.correct: Salt glands on the leaves of Avicennia secrete excess salt, and the roots of Rhizophora exclude most salt by ultrafiltration.
items.misconception: The roots take up seawater freely because mangroves require large amounts of sodium chloride for their metabolism.
items.why: Students see that mangroves are found only in saline habitats and assume the salt must be needed, in the way that a plant found only in shade needs shade. The distinction between tolerating a condition and requiring it is not obvious. Mangroves are salt-tolerant, not salt-dependent. Their adaptations (ultrafiltration at the roots, salt glands, low cell water potential) are ways of coping with salt, which is a stress, not a nutrient they need in large amounts.
items.specStatementText: Adapted to the non-living conditions: dunes and mangroves
items.random_wrong: Pneumatophores pump salt out of the roots and back into the mud, keeping the sap of the tree free of salt.

items.q: A study reports that brown trout survive in water between about 0 °C and 25 °C and grow fastest between 10 °C and 16 °C. During a hot summer the water temperature in a river rises from 14 °C to 22 °C. Which statement correctly applies the idea of a range of tolerance?
items.correct: 22 °C is inside the trout's range of tolerance but outside its optimum, so the fish survive but are under stress.
items.misconception: 22 °C is outside the trout's range of tolerance, so the population in the river will die out before the end of summer.
items.why: Students learn 'optimum temperature' for enzymes and see graphs of activity collapsing above it, and then meet range of tolerance graphs whose central optimum zone is the only part they attend to. A range of tolerance graph has an optimum zone in the middle, zones of stress on either side, and limits of tolerance at the ends. A species survives across the whole range; abundance is highest at the optimum and falls in the zones of stress.
items.specStatementText: Tolerance ranges decide distribution
items.random_wrong: The trout will adapt during their lifetime, widening their range of tolerance to include the new temperature.

items.q: Which statement about abiotic variables and the distribution of species is correct?
items.correct: Adaptations give a species a range of tolerance for each abiotic variable, and it is absent where a variable is outside that range.
items.misconception: Only the distribution of plants is limited by abiotic variables, because animals are able to move away from unfavourable conditions.
items.why: Fieldwork on species distribution is nearly always done with plants (they stay still), and students think of animals as free agents; moving away is seen as escaping the problem rather than as the abiotic variable determining distribution. Moving away from unfavourable conditions is exactly how an abiotic variable limits an animal's distribution: the animal is absent from places outside its range of tolerance. Trout are absent from warm water, corals from cold water, and freshwater fish from the sea.
items.specStatementText: Tolerance ranges decide distribution
items.random_wrong: A species with a wide range of tolerance for temperature is found everywhere that the temperature lies within that range.

items.q: A student lays a 30 m transect from the seaward edge of a salt marsh up the shore, placing a quadrat every 5 m. In each quadrat they record the percentage cover of sea lavender and measure the salinity of the soil water in parts per thousand (ppt) with a conductivity sensor. The results are: 0 m, salinity 35 ppt, cover 0%; 5 m, 32, 10%; 10 m, 28, 35%; 15 m, 24, 60%; 20 m, 20, 55%; 25 m, 16, 20%; 30 m, 12, 0%. Which conclusion is best supported by these data?
items.correct: Cover peaks at intermediate salinity, consistent with a range of tolerance whose optimum lies near 20 to 24 ppt.
items.misconception: Salinity has no effect on sea lavender, because cover is zero at both the highest and the lowest salinity recorded.
items.why: Correlation is taught through straight-line scatter graphs labelled positive or negative, so students look for a monotonic trend and read anything else as 'no correlation'. The range of tolerance predicts a hump-shaped relationship: absence beyond the lower limit, rising abundance towards the optimum, and falling abundance to absence beyond the upper limit. Such a pattern in transect data is strong evidence that the variable affects the distribution.
items.specStatementText: Finding a limit with a transect
items.random_wrong: The transect proves that salinity is the cause of the distribution, because cover changes wherever salinity changes.

items.q: Students are required to collect transect data from a natural or semi-natural habitat. Which of these sites is semi-natural?
items.correct: A hay meadow that is cut once each year but is dominated by wild grasses and wildflowers.
items.misconception: A field of wheat grown from sown seed, with wild poppies growing along its margins.
items.why: Students latch on to 'wild species' in the definition and treat presence as the criterion, overlooking the word 'dominated'. A semi-natural habitat is dominated by wild species. Wild poppies along the edge of a wheat field do not change the fact that the field is dominated by a cultivated crop.
items.specStatementText: Finding a limit with a transect
items.random_wrong: A garden lawn sown with a bought seed mixture and mown every week through the summer.

items.q: A student wants to find out whether the distribution of dog's mercury, a woodland plant, is correlated with light intensity across the boundary between a field and a wood. Which procedure is most appropriate?
items.correct: Place quadrats at regular intervals along a transect from the field into the wood, recording percentage cover and a light-sensor reading at each quadrat.
items.misconception: Place quadrats at random coordinates within the wood only, because the field contains no dog's mercury and so gives no useful data.
items.why: Students see fieldwork as recording the organism, so an empty quadrat feels like a failed sample rather than a data point; they do not think of absence as information. To correlate distribution with an abiotic variable, quadrats must span the whole range of the variable, including places where the species is absent. Without the zeros there is no contrast to correlate.
items.specStatementText: Finding a limit with a transect
items.random_wrong: Record the species present in one large quadrat in the field and one large quadrat in the wood, since two contrasting sites are enough to show a correlation.

items.q: Which statement about the conditions needed for a coral reef to form is correct?
items.correct: The water must be shallow and clear enough for light to reach the zooxanthellae in the coral tissue.
items.misconception: The water must be deep, so that the coral polyps are shielded from the damaging effects of bright sunlight.
items.why: Corals are animals, and students picture animals on the sea floor of the deep ocean; the dependence of reef corals on photosynthetic partners inside their tissues is not intuitive. Reef-building corals depend on zooxanthellae, photosynthetic algae in their tissues, for much of their carbon. Photosynthesis needs light, so reefs are restricted to shallow, clear water; below the depth light reaches, reef corals cannot grow.
items.specStatementText: What a coral reef needs
items.random_wrong: The water should be turbid and rich in suspended sediment, which supplies food to the polyps.

items.q: Reef-building corals deposit skeletons of calcium carbonate. As the oceans absorb more carbon dioxide, the average pH of surface seawater has fallen from about 8.2 to 8.1 and the concentration of carbonate ions has decreased. Which statement best explains why this threatens the formation of coral reefs?
items.correct: Fewer carbonate ions are available, so calcification slows and may not keep pace with reef erosion.
items.misconception: Seawater at pH 8.1 is acidic, so it dissolves the calcium carbonate of existing coral skeletons directly.
items.why: The name 'acidification' and news images of shells dissolving in acid lead students to picture the sea as an acid; they do not check the value against the pH scale. Ocean acidification is a fall in pH from about 8.2 to about 8.1: the water remains alkaline. The harm to reefs comes mainly from the reduced concentration of carbonate ions, which slows calcification, not from acid dissolving skeletons.
items.specStatementText: What a coral reef needs
items.random_wrong: The extra dissolved carbon dioxide is toxic to the coral polyps, which die before they can deposit any skeleton.

items.q: A biome distribution graph has mean annual temperature on one axis and mean annual precipitation on the other. Region X has a mean annual temperature of 26 °C and 150 mm of precipitation a year; region Y has a mean annual temperature of 26 °C and 3000 mm a year. What does the graph predict?
items.correct: Hot desert is likely to develop in region X and tropical forest in region Y, because rainfall separates them at this temperature.
items.misconception: Tropical forest is likely in both regions, because it is the temperature of 26 °C that determines which biome forms.
items.why: Biomes are commonly introduced as bands running from the equator to the poles, and temperature is the variable students associate with latitude, so rainfall drops out of the picture. The biome graph has two axes for a reason: mean annual temperature and mean annual precipitation together predict the ecosystem type. Hot desert and tropical forest can share a temperature of 26 °C; it is rainfall that separates them.
items.specStatementText: Temperature and rainfall set the biome
items.random_wrong: Grassland is likely in region X and tropical forest in region Y, because grassland forms wherever it is too dry for trees.

items.q: Cacti of the deserts of the Americas and euphorbias of the deserts of southern Africa both have swollen, water-storing stems and spines, yet they belong to different plant families. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: Similar abiotic conditions selected for similar adaptations in unrelated lineages, an example of convergent evolution.
items.misconception: The similar appearance shows that cacti and euphorbias share a recent common ancestor that spread to both continents.
items.why: Students learn that similarity indicates relatedness when classification is introduced, and extend this to all similarity, not just similarity in features inherited from a common ancestor. Cacti (Americas) and euphorbias (Africa) belong to different families; their spines and swollen stems evolved independently. Convergent evolution is one reason why the ecosystems of a biome have similar communities although the species differ.
items.specStatementText: Biomes: similar conditions, similar communities
items.random_wrong: Hot desert is one biome, so its community is the same on every continent and each plant in it has the desert form.

items.q: A biome has long, very cold winters, a growing season of only a few weeks, precipitation below about 250 mm a year and permanently frozen subsoil. Which biome is this?
items.correct: Tundra, as in Arctic Canada
items.misconception: Taiga, as in northern Canada
items.why: The two names are unfamiliar, both begin with 't', and both are placed in the far north on biome maps, so students treat them as one cold biome. Taiga is coniferous forest with long, cold winters and short, mild summers. Tundra lies beyond the tree line: very cold, a growing season of a few weeks, very low precipitation and permanently frozen subsoil, supporting only low-growing plants.
items.specStatementText: Biomes: similar conditions, similar communities
items.random_wrong: Hot desert, as in Arabia

items.q: The saguaro cactus (Carnegiea gigantea) of the Sonoran Desert has spines instead of leaves, a thick waxy cuticle, a pleated stem that swells after rain, and roots that are shallow but spread widely. Which statement about these adaptations is correct?
items.correct: Spines in place of leaves reduce the surface area from which water is lost by transpiration.
items.misconception: The spines are a defence against herbivores and play no part in reducing the water that the plant loses.
items.why: Spines are sharp, and their obvious effect on anyone who touches a cactus is the one students remember; that spines are the plant's leaves, and what that means for transpiration, is not visible. In the saguaro the leaves have been reduced to spines and photosynthesis takes place in the green stem. The tiny surface area of spines compared with leaves greatly reduces water loss, which is the primary adaptation; defence against herbivores is an additional benefit.
items.specStatementText: Named species in hot desert and rainforest
items.random_wrong: The waxy cuticle absorbs dew that condenses on the stem at night, and this is the plant's main source of water.

items.q: The fennec fox (Vulpes zerda) lives in the Sahara. It has very large ears with many blood vessels close to the surface, it is active at night and it rarely drinks. How do the large ears help the fox to survive in a hot desert?
items.correct: Heat is radiated from blood flowing near the surface of the ears, cooling the fox without any loss of water.
items.misconception: The ears detect prey moving beneath the sand; their size has nothing to do with body temperature.
items.why: Ears are known as organs of hearing, and the fennec is often described as 'listening for prey under the sand', so the thermoregulatory role of a large, thin, vascular surface is not considered. Large, thin ears richly supplied with blood are a heat-radiating surface. This matters in a hot desert because it cools the animal without evaporating water, which is the scarce resource; hearing prey is a second function of the same structure.
items.specStatementText: Named species in hot desert and rainforest
items.random_wrong: The ears sweat heavily, and the evaporation of this sweat is the fox's main way of losing heat.

items.q: The kapok tree (Ceiba pentandra) grows to over 60 m in tropical rainforest, where rainfall exceeds 2000 mm a year and soils are shallow and poor in nutrients because most nutrients are held in living biomass. Which is an adaptation of the kapok to these conditions?
items.correct: Buttress roots that spread out above the ground and support the tall trunk in the shallow soil.
items.misconception: Rolled leaves lined with hairs that trap humid air and reduce water lost by transpiration.
items.why: Hot desert and tropical rainforest are taught together and both are hot; students carry the desert framework across and expect every adaptation to be about saving water. Rainforest adaptations include buttress roots to support tall trees in shallow soil, drip tips that shed water from leaf surfaces, rapid growth towards light, and prehensile tails and long limbs for life in the canopy. None of these conserves water, because water is not the limiting resource.
items.specStatementText: Named species in hot desert and rainforest
items.random_wrong: A deep taproot that reaches the water table far below the shallow layer of nutrient-poor soil.

items.q: The black-handed spider monkey (Ateles geoffroyi) lives in the canopy of Central American rainforest, feeding mainly on ripe fruit. Which statement about its prehensile tail is correct?
items.correct: It is an inherited adaptation to moving and feeding in the canopy, where it acts as a fifth limb.
items.misconception: Each monkey develops a grasping tail by practice in its life and passes the change to its young.
items.why: In everyday English 'adapt' means to adjust, as a person adapts to a new job, so students read 'adaptations of organisms' as things organisms do rather than features they inherit. Acclimatization to heat or altitude reinforces the idea. Adaptations are inherited features produced by natural selection acting on populations over generations. A species' range of tolerance is a property of its inherited adaptations; individuals cannot extend it by effort or exposure.
items.specStatementText: Named species in hot desert and rainforest
items.random_wrong: It was selected for because shortage of water in the canopy is the main pressure on rainforest animals.

items.q: Off the mouth of a large river such as the Amazon, the coastal seawater is warm and shallow, but it is diluted by fresh water from the river and carries a heavy load of suspended sediment. Reef-building corals are absent from this water. Which statement correctly explains their absence?
items.correct: River water lowers the salinity below the range corals tolerate and its sediment reduces the clarity of the water.
items.misconception: Salinity is irrelevant because any seawater is salty enough for corals; only the sediment from the river prevents reef formation.
items.why: Students learn that the sea is uniformly salty and that reefs need warm, shallow water, so salinity is not seen as a variable at all; the dilution of coastal water by rivers is not obvious from a map. Salinity is one of the five conditions for reef formation. Coastal waters near large river mouths are both diluted and turbid, and reefs are absent from them even where the water is warm and shallow.
items.specStatementText: What a coral reef needs
items.random_wrong: The sediment carried by the river is a benefit, supplying food to the polyps; reefs are absent only because the water is too fresh.

items.q: Must a habitat be a large region such as a whole biome?
items.correct: No. A habitat is the place in which a particular community, species, population or organism lives; it can be as large as an ocean or as small as the underside of a single stone.
items.misconception: A habitat is a large region of the Earth with one type of climate, such as 'the rainforest' or 'the desert'.
items.why: Children's books and documentaries label whole biomes as 'habitats' ('the rainforest habitat'), so students equate the two words and expect a habitat to be a large climatic region. A biome is a group of ecosystems with similar communities and abiotic conditions. A habitat is the place where a specific organism, population or community lives, described by geographical and physical location and ecosystem type; a rainforest biome contains many different habitats.
items.specStatementText: Habitat is the place, not the role or the residents
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a habitat the same thing as the community that lives there?
items.correct: No. The habitat is the place; the community is all the populations of different species that live and interact there.
items.misconception: A habitat is the collection of organisms living together in an area.
items.why: Habitats are usually introduced by listing the organisms found in them ('a rock pool habitat contains limpets, anemones and crabs'), so students attach the word to the organisms rather than to the place. The habitat is the place in which the community lives, described by location and ecosystem type. The organisms that live there make up the community, which together with the habitat's abiotic environment forms an ecosystem.
items.specStatementText: Habitat is the place, not the role or the residents
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the purpose of transpiration to keep a plant cool?
items.correct: No. Transpiration is an unavoidable consequence of opening stomata to take in carbon dioxide; although evaporation does cool the leaf, plants in dry habitats have adaptations to reduce transpiration because water loss threatens survival.
items.misconception: Plants lose water through their leaves in order to cool down, in the way that animals sweat, so a plant in a hot or dry place benefits from losing more water.
items.why: Transpiration is often compared with sweating, and students learn that evaporation has a cooling effect, so they treat water loss as something the plant does deliberately for its own benefit. In a dry habitat such as a sand dune or a hot desert, water is the scarce resource. Adaptations such as rolled leaves, hairs that trap humid air, thick cuticles and spines in place of leaves all act to reduce transpiration, not to increase it.
items.specStatementText: Adapted to the non-living conditions: dunes and mangroves
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do plants adapted to dry habitats keep their stomata permanently closed?
items.correct: No. Stomata must open at some point to let carbon dioxide in for photosynthesis; adaptations reduce the water lost while they are open, or restrict opening to cooler times such as the night.
items.misconception: A plant adapted to dry conditions stops all water loss by keeping its stomata shut all the time.
items.why: Students learn that closing stomata prevents water loss and that dry-habitat plants are 'good at saving water', so they extend the idea to an absolute: no opening, no loss. A plant that never opened its stomata could not take in carbon dioxide and would starve. Marram grass reduces the loss from open stomata by trapping humid air inside the rolled leaf; the saguaro cactus opens its stomata at night when it is cooler. Water loss is reduced, not abolished.
items.specStatementText: Adapted to the non-living conditions: dunes and mangroves
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How do mangroves get rid of the excess salt they take up from seawater?
items.correct: By secreting it from salt glands on the leaves (Avicennia), or by preventing most of it from entering in the first place through ultrafiltration at the roots (Rhizophora).
items.misconception: Excess salt is pumped back out of the roots into the mud or seawater.
items.why: Students reason that salt enters through the roots so it must leave the same way, and pumping it 'back into the sea' seems the obvious route; the leaves are not thought of as a site for excretion. Salt cannot be pumped back into the very salty water around the roots without a large energy cost. Avicennia moves salt to the leaves and secretes it onto the leaf surface from salt glands, where rain and wind remove it; Rhizophora excludes most salt at the root by ultrafiltration. Pneumatophores are for gas exchange, not salt removal.
items.specStatementText: Adapted to the non-living conditions: dunes and mangroves
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: If the temperature of a place lies within a species' range of tolerance, will the species be found there?
items.correct: Not necessarily. Every abiotic variable (water, light, pH, salinity, oxygen and others) must lie within the species' range of tolerance, and even then biotic factors or barriers to dispersal may exclude it.
items.misconception: A species is found everywhere that one abiotic variable, such as temperature, lies within its range of tolerance.
items.why: Range of tolerance is introduced with one variable at a time, usually temperature, so students treat that single variable as sufficient and forget that the others must also be suitable. Distribution is limited by whichever abiotic variable is outside the range of tolerance. A place with suitable temperature may still be too dry, too dark, too saline or too acidic for the species.
items.specStatementText: Tolerance ranges decide distribution
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What counts as an abiotic variable?
items.correct: A non-living physical or chemical factor of the environment, such as temperature, water availability, light intensity, pH, salinity or dissolved oxygen concentration.
items.misconception: An abiotic variable is any environmental factor that varies from place to place, including the presence of predators, food or competitors.
items.why: The word 'abiotic' is unfamiliar and students remember it only as 'environmental factor', losing the 'non-living' meaning of the prefix; predators and food are obviously important to distribution, so they are swept into the same category. Abiotic means non-living. Predation, competition, food availability and disease are biotic factors. Abiotic variables that affect distribution include temperature, water, light, soil or water pH, salinity, mineral nutrients and, for aquatic animals, dissolved oxygen.
items.specStatementText: Tolerance ranges decide distribution
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a correlation between a species' distribution and an abiotic variable along a transect prove that the variable causes the distribution?
items.correct: No. A correlation is consistent with causation but does not prove it: another variable that changes along the same transect, or a biotic factor, could be responsible. Establishing cause requires an experiment in which the variable is manipulated.
items.misconception: If cover changes in step with an abiotic variable along a transect, that variable must be the cause of the distribution.
items.why: The transect is set up to test a specific variable, so a matching pattern feels like confirmation, and students have not usually been asked to name the other things that change along the same line (moisture, salinity, trampling, competition). Transect data can only correlate distribution with an abiotic variable. Up a shore, salinity, exposure, time submerged, soil moisture and competition all change together, so a correlation with any one of them is not proof that it is the limiting factor.
items.specStatementText: Finding a limit with a transect
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is any rural or green site a semi-natural habitat?
items.correct: No. A semi-natural habitat is one influenced by humans but dominated by wild rather than cultivated species. Crop fields, lawns and flower beds are dominated by cultivated species and are not semi-natural.
items.misconception: Fields, parks and gardens are semi-natural habitats because they are outdoors and green.
items.why: Students equate 'natural' with 'not built on', so a wheat field or a mown lawn looks like countryside and therefore semi-natural; the criterion of which species dominate is not what they notice. The test is whether the species that dominate the site are wild or cultivated. A hay meadow of wild grasses cut once a year is semi-natural; a sown lawn or a wheat field is dominated by cultivated species and is not.
items.specStatementText: Finding a limit with a transect
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does human influence on a habitat make it unsuitable for collecting transect data?
items.correct: No. The guide asks for a natural or semi-natural habitat, and a semi-natural habitat is by definition one that has been influenced by humans but is dominated by wild species; such sites are entirely suitable.
items.misconception: Only habitats untouched by humans are acceptable, so any site with a history of management does not count.
items.why: Students hear 'natural habitat' and assume the requirement is for pristine wilderness; they do not realize that 'semi-natural' was included precisely so that managed sites dominated by wild species can be used. A natural habitat is untouched by human management; a semi-natural habitat has been influenced by humans (grazing, mowing, coppicing) but is dominated by wild species. Both are suitable, and semi-natural sites are usually the ones available to students.
items.specStatementText: Finding a limit with a transect
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are two contrasting sites enough to show that a species' distribution is correlated with an abiotic variable?
items.correct: No. Two points can always be joined by a line; a correlation needs many sampling points across the range of the variable, which is why quadrats are placed at regular intervals along a transect.
items.misconception: Comparing one sample from each of two different areas is enough to show a correlation.
items.why: Students have compared two conditions in controlled experiments and carry the 'two treatments' design over into fieldwork, not recognizing that a gradient must be sampled at many points. A transect samples the abiotic variable and the species at many points along a gradient, so that the pattern of change can be seen. Two sites give a difference, not a correlation.
items.specStatementText: Finding a limit with a transect
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does an abiotic variable such as light intensity have a single value across a habitat?
items.correct: No. Abiotic variables change from place to place within a habitat (light falls sharply from a field into a wood, salinity changes up a shore), which is exactly why they are measured at every sampling point along a transect.
items.misconception: An abiotic variable is a fixed property of a habitat, so one measurement is enough to describe it.
items.why: Weather reports give a single temperature for a whole town, and textbook descriptions give a biome a single climate, so students think of abiotic conditions as uniform over an area. The variation of an abiotic variable along a transect is what the investigation relies on. Sensors are used to measure temperature, light intensity or soil pH at each quadrat, so that each value can be paired with the abundance of the species there.

items.q: Is turbid, sediment-rich water good for coral reefs?
items.correct: No. Suspended sediment reduces the light reaching the zooxanthellae and can settle on and smother the polyps, so reefs need clear water; they do not form where rivers bring in sediment.
items.misconception: Cloudy water full of particles is good for corals because it provides more food for them to filter out.
items.why: Students learn that coral polyps capture food from the water with their tentacles and reason that more particles means more food, as for filter feeders such as mussels. Polyps do capture zooplankton at night, but most of the coral's carbon comes from its zooxanthellae, which need light. Clarity is one of the conditions for reef formation because sediment blocks light and smothers the polyps.
items.specStatementText: What a coral reef needs
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is warmer water always better for coral reefs?
items.correct: No. Reef-building corals have a range of tolerance for temperature, typically about 23 to 29 °C; water that is too warm causes stress and bleaching, just as water that is too cold prevents reef formation.
items.misconception: Corals are tropical, so the warmer the water the faster the reef grows.
items.why: Students learn that reefs need warm water and that reaction rates rise with temperature, and extrapolate without an upper limit; they may also know reefs are absent from cold seas and infer that only cold is a problem. Temperature is a limiting factor with both a lower and an upper limit. Reefs form in warm water within the corals' range of tolerance; when water stays a degree or two above the normal summer maximum for weeks, corals expel their zooxanthellae and bleach.
items.specStatementText: What a coral reef needs
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is dissolved carbon dioxide toxic to coral polyps?
items.correct: No, not at the concentrations found in seawater. The threat from rising carbon dioxide is chemical: it lowers pH and reduces the carbonate ion concentration available for calcification.
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide is a pollutant that poisons the coral animals.
items.why: Carbon dioxide is presented as the villain of climate change and students assign it the properties of a toxin, rather than tracing the actual chemistry of its reaction with water. Carbon dioxide reacts with water to form carbonic acid, which releases hydrogen ions; these combine with carbonate ions, lowering their concentration. Corals need carbonate ions to deposit calcium carbonate, so calcification slows. The polyps are not poisoned.

items.q: Is a fall of 0.1 pH units too small to matter?
items.correct: No. The pH scale is logarithmic, so a fall of 0.1 units is an increase of about 26% in hydrogen ion concentration, enough to reduce carbonate ion concentration and slow calcification measurably.
items.misconception: A change of 0.1 on the pH scale is a tiny change in acidity that no organism could detect.
items.why: Students treat the pH scale as linear, like a ruler, and judge the size of a change by the size of the number; the logarithmic nature of pH is learned in chemistry and not carried into biology. Each whole unit of pH is a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration, so 0.1 unit is a factor of about 1.26. The observed fall has already lowered carbonate ion availability and is a genuine limiting factor for reef formation.

items.q: Does grassland develop wherever rainfall is too low for forest?
items.correct: No. Grassland develops where rainfall is too low for forest but still enough for grasses, roughly 250 to 750 mm a year in temperate regions; where rainfall falls below about 250 mm, desert develops instead.
items.misconception: Anywhere too dry for trees becomes grassland.
items.why: Grassland is often described in one line as 'where it is too dry for forest', and the lower boundary with desert is not stated, so students extend grassland down to zero rainfall. On the biome graph grassland occupies an intermediate band of precipitation. Below it, at less than about 250 mm a year, lies desert; above it lies forest. A region with 150 mm of rain a year and a mean temperature of 26 °C is hot desert.
items.specStatementText: Temperature and rainfall set the biome
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a biome determined by latitude or by the continent it is on?
items.correct: No. Biome distribution is determined by abiotic factors, chiefly temperature and rainfall pattern. Latitude matters only insofar as it affects climate, and the same biome occurs on several continents wherever the climate is similar.
items.misconception: The biome is fixed by where a place is on the globe, so you cannot predict it from climate alone.
items.why: Maps of biomes look like maps of latitude bands and continents, so students memorize 'rainforest at the equator' and 'tundra in the far north' as geographical facts rather than as consequences of climate. For any given temperature and rainfall pattern, one natural ecosystem type is likely to develop, wherever on Earth it occurs. That is why tropical forest is found in South America, Africa and south-east Asia, and why deserts occur at many latitudes.
items.specStatementText: Temperature and rainfall set the biome
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do all the ecosystems in a biome contain the same species?
items.correct: No. The ecosystems of a biome have similar community structure and similar types of adaptation, produced by similar abiotic conditions and convergent evolution, but the species are usually different on different continents.
items.misconception: A biome is the same everywhere: the rainforest in Africa contains the same species as the rainforest in South America.
items.why: Biomes are described by their general appearance and climate, and students assume the same look implies the same species, especially when a biome is presented with a single set of example organisms. A biome is a group of ecosystems with similar communities, not identical ones. Jaguars in South America and leopards in Africa fill similar roles in tropical forest, but they are different species that evolved separately.
items.specStatementText: Biomes: similar conditions, similar communities
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is any region with very low precipitation a hot desert?
items.correct: No. Very low precipitation is characteristic of both hot deserts and tundra; what distinguishes them is temperature. Hot deserts have very high daytime temperatures, whereas tundra has mean annual temperatures below freezing.
items.misconception: Desert means dry, so any place with under 250 mm of rain a year is a hot desert.
items.why: Desert is defined to students by rainfall alone, and the image of a desert is always hot sand, so the temperature axis of the biome graph is ignored. On the biome graph, low precipitation runs across the whole temperature range: at high temperature it gives hot desert, at very low temperature it gives tundra. Both axes are needed to identify the biome.
items.specStatementText: Biomes: similar conditions, similar communities

items.q: Do desert mammals such as the fennec fox keep cool mainly by sweating?
items.correct: No. Sweating loses water, which is the scarcest resource in a hot desert. The fennec relies on radiating heat from its ears, on being nocturnal, and on sheltering in a burrow by day.
items.misconception: All mammals cool down by sweating, so a desert mammal must sweat a great deal.
items.why: Students generalize from humans, who sweat profusely, to all mammals, and do not weigh the cost of the water lost in a habitat where water is limiting. Water conservation is central to survival in a hot desert. Desert mammals minimize evaporative cooling and instead avoid heat (nocturnal activity, burrows) and lose heat by radiation from surfaces such as large ears.
items.specStatementText: Named species in hot desert and rainforest

items.q: Do desert animals store water in fat deposits such as a camel's hump?
items.correct: No. A hump or other fat deposit stores fat, which is an energy reserve. Metabolizing fat does release some water, but it is not a water store; desert animals conserve water mainly through concentrated urine and by avoiding heat.
items.misconception: Desert animals have fatty structures that store water for use when there is nothing to drink.
items.why: The story that a camel's hump holds water is widespread in children's books, and students transfer the idea to any prominent structure on a desert animal. Fat is an energy store. Desert mammals such as the fennec fox obtain most of their water from food, produce highly concentrated urine, and avoid the heat of the day, rather than storing water in body structures.
items.specStatementText: Named species in hot desert and rainforest

items.q: Do the tallest rainforest trees have deep taproots to reach water far underground?
items.correct: No. Rainforest soils are shallow and most nutrients are in the surface litter, so emergent trees such as the kapok have shallow, wide-spreading roots and are held up by buttress roots at the base of the trunk.
items.misconception: A very tall tree must have a deep taproot to anchor it and to reach water deep in the ground.
items.why: Students know that some plants have long taproots and reason that a taller plant needs a proportionally deeper root, just as a taller building needs deeper foundations. Buttress roots are the kapok's solution to supporting a 60 m trunk in shallow soil: they spread the load over a wide area at the surface. Water is not scarce in rainforest, so there is no selective advantage in reaching deep groundwater.
